doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: His book, Legos and being easy to work with
summary: Ricker talks about his book's lessons: Legos as career building blocks and personality skills such as being good to hang with.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Now you spoke at length about that in this marvelous book that I’ll —
And technology changes so fast that I see you brought on someone to help out with the second edition for that specific purpose.

There was a couple of things in there that I really related to. You mentioned about there’s no lack of great players, and you could have two people who you could hire that played equally well that could both fulfill the task, and you said, “Make sure you don’t act like a jerk because no one’s going to pick you even if you play really well.”

Well that’s true. That’s true. People recommend people who are good players and who are friends of theirs. It’s just normal. You know why do you hire somebody and think that oh man, is this guy going to show up? You know. Or, will there be some incident that will happen? Or if he can go with the flow and, you know, not cause a scene. But there are, you mentioned earlier, before we started taping here, about Legos and Legos are things I talk about like things that you learn in life and how you take these Legos and you put them together and you build a career. And if you get to — the great thing about it is if you build something and then you say hmm, it’s not looking too good, I need to build a little more over here, so you can craft this thing to fit you. Or you can knock the whole thing down and start over you know. But so to me Legos are things you can do. You know you can play certain pieces on your instrument, you gain experience playing in bigger ensembles in orchestras and that kind of thing. But there are also personality Legos that help you. And one of those things is being personable with, you know, with others.
You have to learn how to hang.
That’s right. You’ve got to get the hang down.
I think that should be a course at Eastman, Hang 101.
Yeah. Boy I tell you when I was younger we used to — I could have taught it easily.
